title: Which Hasse derivatives of Xᵐ survive over 𝔽_p — a base-p digit criterion
content: The parent's dichotomy says the ordinary multiplicity test is exact for m < p and blind for m ≥ p. Its open question asks to stratify the blind regime by the base-p digits of m. Since hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) = C(m,k)·X^(m-k), the k-th Hasse derivative is nonzero over 𝔽_p exactly when p ∤ C(m,k), and Lucas's theorem makes that a per-digit statement: hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) ≠ 0 iff every base-p digit of k is ≤ the corresponding digit of m. The surviving orders are the digit-dominated k, which for m ≥ p reach all the way to k = m.
mathContext: $\mathrm{hasseDeriv}\,k\,(X^m) \ne 0$ over a field of characteristic $p$ $\iff \neg\,p \mid \binom{m}{k} \iff \forall i,\ \lfloor k/p^i\rfloor \bmod p \le \lfloor m/p^i\rfloor \bmod p$ (Lucas/Kummer digit domination).

title: Closed form: hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) is a single monomial C(m,k)·X^(m-k)
content: hasseDeriv_X_pow writes X^m as monomial m 1 and applies hasseDeriv_monomial (hasseDeriv k (monomial n r) = monomial (n-k) (C(n,k)·r)), giving hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) = monomial (m-k) (C(m,k)). This collapses the differential operator into one binomial coefficient — the object whose behaviour mod p the whole entry analyses. It holds over any commutative (indeed semiring) R, with no ordering on k, m.

title: Vanishing criterion: nonzero ↔ ¬ p ∣ C(m,k)
content: hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff: over a field F of characteristic p, hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) ≠ 0 ↔ ¬ p ∣ C(m,k). The monomial C(m,k)·X^(m-k) is zero iff its coefficient is (monomial_eq_zero_iff), and the cast (C(m,k) : F) vanishes iff p ∣ C(m,k) (CharP.cast_eq_zero_iff). hasseDeriv_X_pow_eq_zero_iff is the contrapositive packaging. This is the bridge from polynomials to number theory.

title: Single-digit engine: for a < p, ¬ p ∣ C(a,b) ↔ b ≤ a
content: not_dvd_choose_of_le_of_lt_prime shows p ∤ C(a,b) when b ≤ a < p: from C(a,b)·b!·(a-b)! = a! (choose_mul_factorial_mul_factorial), p ∣ C(a,b) would force p ∣ a!, contradicting Nat.Prime.dvd_factorial (p ∤ a! since a < p). not_dvd_choose_digit_iff upgrades this to an iff for a < p, using choose_eq_zero_of_lt for b > a. This is the atomic per-digit fact Lucas multiplies across positions.
mathContext: For $a < p$ prime: $\neg\,p \mid \binom{a}{b} \iff b \le a$, from $\binom{a}{b}\,b!\,(a-b)! = a!$ and $p \nmid a!$.

title: Capstone: the Lucas digit-domination survival criterion
content: hasseDeriv_X_pow_ne_zero_iff_digits: over a field of characteristic p, with m, k < p^a, hasseDeriv k (Xᵐ) ≠ 0 ↔ ∀ i < a, ⌊k/pⁱ⌋ mod p ≤ ⌊m/pⁱ⌋ mod p. The proof rewrites nonvanishing as ¬ p ∣ C(m,k), invokes Lucas's product congruence C(m,k) ≡ ∏ C(mᵢ,kᵢ) (mod p) (Nat.Choose.choose_modEq_prod_range_choose_nat), transfers divisibility across the congruence, distributes the prime with Prime.dvd_finset_prod_iff, and discharges each digit factor with the single-digit engine. This is the exact stratification the open question requested.
mathContext: $\mathrm{hasseDeriv}\,k\,(X^m) \ne 0 \iff \forall i < a,\ \lfloor k/p^i\rfloor \bmod p \le \lfloor m/p^i\rfloor \bmod p$ (every base-$p$ digit of $k$ dominated by that of $m$).

title: 𝔽₂ realization: X³ = 11₂ keeps all four orders
content: nonzero_orders_X3_F2: over 𝔽₂, hasseDeriv k (X³) ≠ 0 ↔ k ≤ 3. Since 3 = 11₂ has digits (1,1), every k ≤ 3 is digit-dominated, so all four orders survive — the Glaisher/Fine count ∏(dᵢ+1) = 2·2 = 4. Orders k > 3 die by hasseDeriv_eq_zero_of_lt_natDegree (degree 3); the four surviving orders are confirmed by interval_cases and kernel decide.

title: 𝔽₂ realization: X⁴ = 100₂ keeps only orders 0 and 4
content: nonzero_orders_X4_F2 and hasseDeriv_X4_F2_profile: over 𝔽₂, hasseDeriv k (X⁴) is nonzero exactly for k ∈ {0,4} and vanishes for k = 1,2,3. Since 4 = 100₂ has digits (0,0,1), only k whose low digits are 0 survive — count ∏(dᵢ+1) = 1·1·2 = 2. This contrasts sharply with X³: survival in the m ≥ p regime is a genuine digit phenomenon, dense or sparse according to the base-p expansion, not a uniform collapse.
mathContext: $4 = 100_2$: only $k \in \{0,4\}$ dominate, count $\prod(d_i+1) = 1\cdot 1\cdot 2 = 2$; the middle orders $k=1,2,3$ vanish over $\mathbb{F}_2$.
